lena.name: Dr. Lena Reyes
lena.role: field biologist (a scientist who studies animals in the wild)

case.title: The Washed-Out Notebook
case.hook: On a boardwalk at a Florida wildlife refuge, I found an old field notebook, soaked by the rain. Most pages are ruined. But four photos of one tall pink bird survived, with notes about its body parts. The last line is washed out.
case.smudge: This bird finds food it can’t even see by…
case.question: How does this bird find food it can’t even see?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

stills.time: flat and wide at the tip
stills.alt: A pink bird with a long, flat beak that widens into a round spoon shape at the tip.
The bird bends its head down and holds its beak in shallow water.
Pink birds standing on long legs in shallow water, one with its beak under the water.
A group of pink birds standing on a sandbar in a shallow lagoon, with mangrove trees behind them.

case.stillsCredit: Real photos, standing in for the notebook’s pages. Beak: roseate spoonbill at Orlando Wetlands Park, Florida, JeffreyGammon (CC BY 4.0). Beak in the water, and the legs: roseate spoonbills, Russ (CC BY 2.0). Where I found it: roseate spoonbills on Sanibel Island, Florida, James St. John (CC BY 2.0). All via Wikimedia Commons.

clues.t: Its flat, wide beak works like a spoon. It sweeps side to side through the water and snaps shut on small animals.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: inside or outside?
clues.t: Inside the tip of its beak are tiny touch sensors (an internal structure). The bird can feel food it can’t see.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 3: how deep can you go?
clues.t: Long legs let it wade (walk in water) where short-legged birds can’t stand. It feeds in shallow water, usually less than knee-deep on a grown-up.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: build a hiding head
clues.t: Where a part sits matters. A gator’s nostrils sit high so it can breathe while it hides. The mystery bird’s nostrils sit high too, near its face, far from the beak tip it sweeps through the water.

solve.title: How does the mystery bird find food?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: It flies high and spots its food with sharp eyes.
options.why: Check Clue 2. This bird finds food it can’t see. Spotting food from high up is an eagle’s job.

options.t: It wades into shallow water on long legs, sweeps its flat beak side to side, and feels for small animals with touch sensors in its beak. Its nostrils stay up high, so it keeps breathing.
options.why: Case cracked! It’s a roseate spoonbill. Every part fits its job: legs for wading, a spoon-shaped beak for sweeping, touch sensors for feeling and nostrils up high for breathing. Now write your case report: it’s the questions below.

options.t: It dives deep underwater and spears fish with a pointy beak.
options.why: Check Clues 1 and 3. A spear-shaped beak belongs to the anhinga. This bird has a spoon shape and stands on long legs.

beaks.title: Beak or tool?
todo: Look at the shape of each beak.
Drag the tool with the same shape onto it, or tap the tool and then the beak.

why.t: Scientists often compare body parts to tools. A beak’s shape tells you its job, just like a tool’s shape does.

beaks.hint: Drag a tool onto a beak, or tap a tool and then tap a beak.

birds.name: Roseate spoonbill
birds.alt: Close-up of a roseate spoonbill’s long beak, flat and round at the tip.
birds.job: Flat and wide at the tip, like a spoon. It sweeps side to side through shallow water and snaps shut on shrimp and small fish.

miss.straw: A straw is long and thin with a hole. Look at the spoonbill’s wide, flat tip.
miss.nut: A nutcracker is short and strong. Is this beak short?
miss.spear: A skewer is sharp and pointy. Is this tip pointy, or round and flat?

birds.name: Ruby-throated hummingbird
birds.alt: A tiny hummingbird hovering at a pink flower with its long, thin beak.
birds.job: Long and thin, like a straw. It reaches deep into flowers to sip nectar (the sweet juice inside).

miss.spoon: A spoon is wide at the end. This beak is thin all the way.
miss.nut: A nutcracker is short and thick. This beak is long and thin.
miss.spear: Close! It’s long and thin. But it sips from flowers instead of stabbing fish.

birds.name: Northern cardinal
birds.alt: A red cardinal with a short, thick, cone-shaped orange beak.
birds.job: Short, thick and strong, like a nutcracker. It cracks open hard seeds.

miss.spoon: A spoon is long and flat. This beak is short and thick.
miss.straw: A straw is long and thin. This beak is short and thick.
miss.spear: A skewer is long and sharp. This beak is short and thick.

birds.name: Anhinga
birds.alt: A dark water bird with a long neck and a long, sharp, pointed beak.
birds.job: Long, straight and sharp, like a skewer. It swims underwater and stabs fish.

miss.spoon: A spoon is round at the end. This tip is sharp.
miss.straw: A straw sips. This beak is sharp and strong. What would it do to a fish?
miss.nut: A nutcracker is short. This beak is long and sharp.

beaks.credit: Roseate spoonbill, Andrea Westmoreland (CC BY-SA 2.0). Ruby-throated hummingbird, Paul Danese (CC BY-SA 4.0). Northern cardinal, Robert Taylor (CC BY 2.0). Anhinga, Russ (CC BY 2.0). All via Wikimedia Commons.
beaks.win: All four matched! Same body part, four shapes, four jobs. That’s a clue: look at what the spoonbill’s spoon does.

judge.title: Inside or outside?
todo: Drag it to a side, or tap a side.
Ask: could I see this part from the outside?
judge.hint: Pick a side for the card above.
judge.miss: Ask: could you see this part from the outside of the living thing?

cards.why: You can see the shell from the outside. It’s external.
Lungs are hidden inside the body. They take in air. They’re internal.

cards.t: A saw palmetto’s big fan-shaped leaves
cards.why: Leaves are on the outside of the plant, catching sunlight. External.

cards.t: The tubes inside a palmetto’s stem that carry water
cards.why: They’re hidden inside the stem. Internal.
Skin covers the outside of the body. External.
The heart is deep inside the body, pumping blood. Internal.
Feathers cover the outside of a bird. External.

cards.t: Tiny touch sensors inside the tip of a spoonbill’s beak
cards.why: They’re hidden inside the beak. These touch sensors let a spoonbill feel a shrimp it can’t see. Internal!
cards.miss: You can see the beak from outside. But are the sensors on the outside, or inside it?

judge.win: All eight sorted! Look at the last card again: that’s a clue about the mystery bird.

wade.title: How deep can you go?
todo: Read what happens to each bird.
Try all four depths, then answer the question.

why.t: Wading means walking through water. Some birds wade to find food, the way you might wade into a pond in tall rubber boots.

wade.start: Tap a water depth to start.

birds.name: Sanderling (short legs)
birds.alt: A small gray-and-white shorebird with short black legs on wet sand.

d1.t: It runs along the wet sand at the edge of the waves, poking for tiny animals.

d6.t: Its short legs can’t reach the bottom here.

d12.t: Much too deep for those short legs.

d36.t: Much too deep. It stays at the edge of the water.

birds.name: Roseate spoonbill (long legs)
birds.alt: A pink spoonbill standing on long legs in dark, shallow water, sweeping its beak.

d1.t: Easy. It sweeps its beak through the shallow water.

d6.t: Still standing! Its long legs keep its body above the water.

d12.t: Still standing. This is near the deepest water it likes to feed in.

d36.t: Even long legs have limits. It can’t stand here and reach the bottom.

birds.name: Mottled duck (short legs, webbed feet)
birds.alt: A brown duck with a yellow bill floating on rippled water.

d1.t: It walks on short legs and dips its bill at the water’s edge.

d6.t: Its legs are too short to stand, so it floats and paddles with its webbed feet.

d12.t: It floats, then tips headfirst to reach food, like a duck doing a handstand.

d36.t: It floats. Food on the bottom is out of reach.

q.q: What do the spoonbill’s long legs let it do?

opts.t: Swim in deep water like a duck
opts.why: The duck floats and paddles with webbed feet. Did the spoonbill float, or stand?

opts.t: Stand and feed in water too deep for short-legged birds, without swimming
opts.why: Yes! Long legs let it wade where short-legged birds can’t stand.
That’s the sanderling at the edge of the waves. What happened when the water got deeper?

wade.credit: Sanderling in Sarasota, Florida, Ryan Hodnett (CC BY-SA 4.0). Roseate spoonbill feeding, Andy Morffew (CC BY 2.0). Mottled duck in Royal Palm Beach, Florida, DickDaniels (CC BY-SA 3.0). All via Wikimedia Commons.
wade.win: That’s a clue about the mystery bird’s long legs.

gator.title: Build a hiding head
todo: Pick where the eyes go and where the nostrils go.
Press Sink it to hide and read the three tests.
Test at least two designs. Then answer the question.

why.t: Scientists can’t move a real gator’s eyes. So they test ideas with a model (a simple copy that shows how something works).

gator.pickFirst: Put the eyes and the nostrils somewhere first.
gator.tryAnother: That one passes! Now test a different design, so you can compare.

tests.yes: Almost the whole head and body are under water. A fish swimming by sees only small bumps.
The eyes stay above the water, so it can watch for a fish or a bird coming close.
tests.no: The eyes are under the water. It can’t watch what’s happening above it.

tests.yes: The nostrils stay above the water, so it can breathe air without moving.
tests.no: The nostrils are under the water. To breathe, it would have to lift its head and give itself away.

gator.alt: A real alligator in a swamp: its head is mostly under the water, with only its eye and the bumps of its nostrils above the surface.
gator.photoCap: The real thing: an American alligator hiding. Its eyes and its nostrils sit on top of its head, so they stay above the water.
gator.credit: American alligator in its hiding position, Mark Herr, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

q.q: Why are a gator’s eyes and nostrils on top of its head?

opts.t: So it can see the sky better
opts.why: Think about the tests. What can it do while its body is under water?

opts.t: Because it chose to put them there
opts.why: Animals don’t choose their parts. Parts that worked well got passed on to babies over many generations.

opts.t: So it can watch and breathe while the rest of its body hides
opts.why: Yes! Where a part sits matters as much as its shape.

gator.win: That’s your last clue. It works for the mystery bird, too.

q1.A: Stems and roots move water. What does a leaf catch from the sky?
q1.C: Holding the plant in the soil is the roots’ job. Which choice is about sunlight?

q2.B: Internal means hidden inside. Can you see a tortoise’s shell from the outside?
q2.C: Invasive means a living thing brought from somewhere else. That’s not about where a part is.

q3.A: Birds don’t choose their beaks for looks. Which answer connects the shape to the job?
q3.C: Spoonbills are native to Florida (they belong here). And that doesn’t explain the shape.

ans-2: Internal means inside the body. External means outside, where you can see it.
Think of the cards you sorted: a shell, lungs, leaves, the tubes in a stem.
Try: An internal structure is ___, like ___. An external structure is ___, like ___.
ans-3: Picture each beak. A hummingbird’s is long and thin. An eagle’s is short, sharp and hooked.
What does each bird eat? Nectar from flowers? Fish and other animals?
Try: Their beaks have different structures because ___. A hummingbird’s beak functions to ___. An eagle’s beak functions to ___.
cer-4: First decide: do you agree or disagree with the classmate?
Look for two plant parts from today and the job each one does.
Try: I ___ because ___. One piece of evidence is ___. Another is ___.

planner.title: Your claim and two pieces of evidence

rows.label: 2. Pick two pieces of evidence from the lesson
options: Leaves catch sunlight so the plant can make its own food.
Roots pull water and nutrients from the soil.
Tubes inside a stem carry water through the plant.
A cactus has sharp spines that keep animals from eating it.
Mangrove roots hold the tree up and take in air.
A Venus flytrap traps insects to get nutrients the soil doesn’t have.

planner.note: Tap your side and two facts. Then write your reasoning in your own words.

welcome.label: Welcome · the washed-out notebook
welcome.script: Hi, it’s Dr. Lena Reyes. This morning I found something on a boardwalk at a Florida wildlife refuge: an old field notebook, soaked by the rain. Most of the pages are ruined. But four photos survived, all of the same tall pink bird. The last line is washed out. It says, this bird finds food it can’t even see by… and then nothing. Look at the photos, then help me find the clues to finish that sentence.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · beak or tool (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Let’s start with the beak, because it’s the strangest part. Scientists often compare body parts to tools, because the shape tells you the job. Look at each beak, then find the tool with the same shape. A tip from the field: don’t look at the bird’s color. Look only at the shape.

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Say each word; for internal and external, point to your own heart, then your own skin.

part2.label: Part 2 · inside or outside (Clue 2)
part2.script: Here’s a field trick. Some of the most important body parts are the ones you can’t see. Sort each card by asking one question: could I see this part from the outside, or is it hidden inside the body? Watch the last card closely. It’s about our mystery bird.

part3.label: Part 3 · how deep can you go (Clue 3)
part3.script: When I work in the marsh, I wear tall rubber boots so I can stand in the water without getting soaked. Some birds have something like that built right into their bodies. Pick a water depth and watch all three birds. Try every depth, and keep an eye on the bird with the longest legs.

explore.label: Part 4 · build a hiding head (Clue 4)
explore.script: Here’s my favorite Florida hider: the American alligator. When I paddle my kayak, sometimes all I see are two bumpy eyes and two little nostrils. Now it’s your turn to build a head. Put the eyes and nostrils where you think they belong, then sink it. Test more than one design. Which one can still watch and breathe?

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: You’ve got all four clues. Before you write, crack the case at the top of this tab: how does the mystery bird find food it can’t see? Then write your case report. Use your clues and the words from today. Your answers save as you type.

partc.label: Part C · label a Florida organism

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says plants don’t really have structures, that they’re just leaves and stems. Hmm. Do you agree? Think about the plants in today’s lesson: the cactus, the mangrove, the flytrap. Pick your side, choose two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.notes: Celebrate; tease 11.02 (build a model that explains how a part works).
closing.script: Case closed! That soggy notebook was about a bird built for feeling, not seeing. Every part of it fits its job. Next time, you’ll turn what you learned into a model, a drawing that explains how a body part does its job. Bring your clues.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how a body part helps a living thing survive?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: A spoonbill sweeps its flat beak through shallow water to feel for shrimp.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “spoonbill”, “flat beak”, “sweeps” and “feel for shrimp”. Those words tell who, which part and what it does. Small words like “a” and “to” don’t carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.

tool.name: X-ray viewer
tool.teaser: A light box and two real X-rays: see the internal structures you can’t see from outside.
tool.done: You read both X-rays and found the hidden parts. An X-ray sticker is in your Field Notebook.

why.t: Internal structures are hidden inside the body. An X-ray lets vets and scientists see bones and other internal parts without hurting the animal.

xray.title: What’s hiding inside?
todo: Pick a film to clip onto the light box.
Tap every number to see what the X-ray shows.
Read both films, then answer the question.

films.name: A turtle, seen from above
films.alt: A gray X-ray of a turtle from above: the outline of the shell, a thin backbone down the middle, leg bones at the corners and three round eggs.
films.credit: X-ray: Uwe Gille, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)
films.intro: This is a real X-ray of a pet turtle. Tap the numbers.

spots.label: Three eggs
spots.t: This turtle was carrying three eggs! A vet took this X-ray to check on them. You could never see them from the outside.

spots.label: Backbone
spots.t: The thin line down the middle is the backbone. In a turtle, the backbone and ribs are joined to the inside of the shell.

spots.label: Shell
spots.t: The edge of the shell. You can see a shell from outside, so it’s external. The X-ray shows it’s made of bone.

spots.label: Leg bones
spots.t: From the outside you see scaly skin. Inside, bones hold the leg up.

films.name: A heron’s neck
films.alt: A gray X-ray of a heron’s long S-shaped neck and head, showing a chain of neck bones, a ringed air tube and a round ring in the eye.
films.credit: X-ray of a heron’s neck, Long Beach Animal Hospital, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain)
films.intro: Herons are wading birds, like spoonbills. Tap the numbers.

spots.label: Neck bones
spots.t: A chain of small neck bones, linked like train cars. They let a heron bend its neck into an S, then shoot its beak forward to grab a fish.

spots.label: Eye ring
spots.t: A ring of tiny bones inside the eye. It helps hold a bird’s big eye in shape.

spots.label: Windpipe
spots.t: The tube with tiny rings is the windpipe, the air tube to the lungs. The rings keep it from squeezing shut.

spots.label: Beak
spots.t: You can see a beak from outside, so it’s external. The X-ray shows the bone inside it, too.

q.q: What can an X-ray show that a regular photo can’t?

opts.why: X-rays are gray. A regular photo shows colors.

opts.t: Internal structures, like bones and eggs, without hurting the animal
opts.why: Yes! That’s why vets and scientists use X-rays: to see hidden parts safely.
An X-ray is a picture, not a recording. What did you see on the films?
